chunks: "A board-level shield is connected to the circuit ground, meaning the PCB ground plane, all the way round its perimeter, either soldered to a ring of ground pads or via a series of ground contacts.
A cable shield or an enclosure is bonded to chassis ground, with the connector shell making a 360 degree, low-inductance contact to the metal enclosure. Why?
A shield stops electric fields by giving the field lines somewhere to terminate and the displacement current somewhere to go.
That current has to return to the source through ground.
If the shield floats, it just takes on a potential set by capacitive dividers, it can be at volts, and then it couples that to whatever's inside, or re-radiates.
And at high frequency the connection impedance matters: 10 nanohenries of pigtail is 6 ohms at 100 megahertz, so the noise current produces a voltage on the shield instead of being drained.
So you want many short, wide connections, spaced under a twentieth of a wavelength.
For cables there's a frequency dependence: at low frequency, grounding a shield at both ends can create a ground loop, so audio shields may be grounded at one end.
At RF, you ground at both ends, and bond to chassis at the connector, so the shield carries the return current and keeps the field in."
